title: Twenty Minutes of Exercise Works as Well as a Nap to Rescue a Sleep-Deprived Brain
excerpt: A McGill University study finds both a short workout and a 90-minute nap boost memory by 22% after 30 hours without sleep — but through different brain pathways.
body:
• A 20-minute cycling session improved memory as effectively as a 90-minute nap after 30 hours of sleep deprivation, a McGill University study found
  • Both interventions boosted memory performance by about 22% compared to doing nothing, according to the research published in PNAS
  • Brain recordings revealed exercise and napping help through different pathways — napping recharges the brain while exercise makes it use remaining resources more efficiently

A short burst of exercise can protect memory just as well as a lengthy nap after a sleepless night, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at McGill University in Montreal.

The findings offer a practical tool for the estimated 40% of the global population that regularly fails to get adequate sleep, and could reshape fatigue-management strategies in high-stakes workplaces from hospitals to cockpits.

The Study Design

Researchers recruited 54 healthy young adults and kept them awake for 30 consecutive hours under controlled lab conditions. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of three groups: a 20-minute moderate-to-vigorous cycling session, a 90-minute nap, or a control group that simply sat still.

After the intervention, all participants viewed 150 images and rated the emotional intensity of each. Three days later, they returned and were shown those 150 images mixed with 75 new ones, and asked to identify which they had seen before.

The results were clear: participants who exercised or napped remembered significantly more images than those who did neither, with both groups performing about 22% better on the recognition task.

“Sleep loss affects nearly every aspect of how we think and function, but many people can’t simply stop what they’re doing and get more sleep. Our findings show that even a brief bout of exercise may help preserve one of our most important cognitive abilities.”

— Marc Roig, Professor, McGill University School of Physical and Occupational Therapy

Same Benefit, Different Mechanisms

While the memory improvements were nearly identical, brain recordings told a more nuanced story. Napping appeared to recharge the brain, making it easier to absorb and retain new information. Exercise, by contrast, helped the brain deploy its remaining resources more efficiently — without making participants feel more drowsy.

That distinction matters for real-world application. A 90-minute nap requires a quiet space and time that may not be available during a shift. Twenty minutes on an exercise bike is far more accessible — and unlike a nap, it does not leave people groggy.

Implications for High-Risk Workplaces

The findings could eventually reshape fatigue-management protocols in healthcare, transportation, emergency response, and military settings — environments where sleep deprivation is common and cognitive errors carry serious consequences.

Shift workers, new parents, and long-haul travelers could also benefit. The study adds to a growing body of evidence, including earlier work from the University of Portsmouth showing that 20 minutes of moderate cycling improved cognitive performance regardless of sleep status or oxygen levels.

Researchers cautioned that the study involved young, healthy participants and that the long-term effects of relying on exercise as a sleep substitute are not yet known. The team plans follow-up studies to test whether the benefits hold for older adults and for people with chronic sleep disorders.
nri_angle: Sleep deprivation is a widespread concern for diaspora professionals and shift workers; the study offers a practical intervention accessible to anyone with 20 minutes.
